belief: Needing medication means my faith is weak.
origins: Some believers are taught that faith and medicine are opposed. Taking pills can then feel like a lack of trust. Guilt sometimes leads people to stop treatment.
teaches: Jesus said, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” Paul counseled Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments. Luke was a physician, and Paul called him “beloved.” The good Samaritan used oil and wine for wounds. “The prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick” (James 5:15), and elders are told to pray and anoint with oil, an ancient medicinal practice. God works through prayer and through doctors and medicine. Using both is wise.
self_statements: A strong believer would trust God alone.
If God is my healer, I should not need pills.
Others are healed by faith alone.
errors: Believing I must choose either faith or medicine.
Predicting that God will withdraw if I use medicine.
Feeling guilty and concluding my faith is weak.
questions: Where did I learn to set faith against medicine?
What does Scripture say about doctors and remedies?
Can I thank God for the medicine He provides?
Who can pray with me as I continue treatment?
What peace could I have in using both?
truth: Faith and medicine work together. God heals through many means, and using medicine wisely is an act of trust and stewardship. I can pray and take my treatment with thanks.
hw_truths: I can give thanks for my treatment.
I will follow my doctor’s advice.
log: Each week, thank God as you take your treatment.
actions: Talk with your pastor and doctor.
Make changes only with your doctor.
prayer: Lord, thank You for medicine and doctors. Free me from guilt, and help me trust You as I use the means You provide. Amen.
